sites.name: HMS King Edward VII

s1.quote: The least echo sounder depth was 94 in a general depth of 108 metres.

summary.text: Pre-dreadnought battleship lost to a German-laid mine in January 1916 and now a large wreck off the north coast, surveyed by side-scan sonar in 1984. At roughly 100 m it is a deep technical dive.

sites.depthNote: Least depth 94 m in 108 m general depth (1984 survey)

sites.name: SMS Dresden (1917)

s1.quote: Max-Depth: 38m … the northward pointing bow sitting in 25 metres. The remainder of the ship slopes southward toward the stern at 38 metres.

s2.quote: She now rests on her port side in a maximum of 38m water at the stern and is largely intact. The northward pointing bow lies in 30m, the shallowest point is around 16m.

highlights.text: Armoured control tower with viewing slits
Original features still inside the hull

summary.text: German light cruiser scuttled in 1919 that lies on her port side on a slope, bow shallow and stern deep, which suits a multi-level dive. Fairly intact, with the control tower and original fittings; often a first dive of a Scapa trip.

sites.depthNote: Bow 25-30 m, stern 38 m, shallowest ~16 m

s1.quote: Max-Depth: 38m … König lies almost completely overturned and has been extensively opened up by the salvage teams.

s2.quote: lying at a depth of 40 m (130 ft) on a sandy floor to the east of Cava . She turned over as she sank and the hull faces upwards at about 20 m (66 ft) down.

highlights.text: Upturned hull opened up by salvage blasting
Casemate guns lying upside down on seabed

hazards.text: Blast debris scattered along the hull

summary.text: Upturned WWI German battleship east of Cava, scuttled in 1919 and heavily broken by salvage blasting. Less impressive than her sisters but the openings reveal internal structure; the hull top is around 20 m.

s1.quote: in 82 metres of water. The wreck lies on its side as is well broken particularly from bow to bridge … The wreck is protected under The Military Remains Act 1986.

s2.quote: The wreck lies roughly E-W, in 82 metres (269 ft) of water

access.value: Protected under the Military Remains Act 1986

hazards.text: Wreck heavily broken from bow to bridge

summary.text: M-class destroyer lost with all hands to a mine west of Hoy in March 1917. She lies on her side in about 82 m, broken forward of the bridge, so it is a deep technical dive on a protected war wreck.

s1.quote: It lies at the mouth of Pan Hope, a large inlet on the east side of Flotta. … the only really identifiable elements aside from plates, pipes, wires and so on are the ballast tanks and a deck gun.

s2.quote: the submarine is very broken up with the conning tower as one of the few remaining identifiable features. The wreck of UB-116 is pretty small, and relatively shallow for Scapa Flow

highlights.text: Conning tower, ballast tanks and deck gun remain

hazards.text: Wreck very broken up after torpedo clearance

summary.text: The last U-boat sunk in WWI, destroyed by a mine in Hoxa Sound in 1918, raised, then lost again at the mouth of Pan Hope off Flotta. Small, shallow for Scapa and badly broken, so an easy second dive.
